title: ECMO and mechanical circulatory support
summary: Advanced module on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV and VA), referral and ECPR, IABP and Impella, daily ECMO rounds, complications and emergencies, and weaning — written so a junior can recognise when to call for help and safely look after an ECMO patient overnight.
authors: ICU 360 content team (AI-drafted, pending consultant review)

topics.title: VV vs VA ECMO: modes and indications
topics.summary: How the two ECMO configurations work, who each is for, contraindications, and the physiology a junior must understand before touching the circuit.

definition.text: ECMO pumps blood through an artificial membrane lung. VV ECMO drains venous blood and returns it oxygenated to the venous side (gas exchange only; relies on the native heart). VA ECMO drains venous blood and returns it into the arterial system (supports circulation and gas exchange, in parallel with the native heart).

steps.title: Name the failing organ
steps.detail: Lungs only with adequate heart function → VV ECMO (gas exchange support). Heart failing (± lungs) → VA ECMO (circulatory + gas exchange support). Do a bedside echo before deciding: severe LV/RV failure on VV may need VA or a hybrid configuration.

steps.title: Optimise conventional care first
steps.detail: Severe ARDS: lung-protective ventilation (VT 6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤30, driving pressure ≤15), PEEP titration, neuromuscular blockade, and prone positioning ≥12–16 h/day unless contraindicated. Shock: fluids if responsive, noradrenaline, inotropes, revascularisation, treat arrhythmia.

steps.title: Check VV indications (ELSO 2021)
steps.detail: Any of: PaO₂/FiO₂ <80 mmHg after optimal care including a prone trial; hypercapnic failure with pH <7.25 despite RR 35/min and Pplat ≤30; bridge to lung transplant. EOLIA entry (used by many centres): P/F <50 for >3 h, P/F <80 for >6 h, or pH <7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥60 mmHg for >6 h despite optimisation.

steps.title: Check VA indications
steps.detail: Refractory cardiogenic shock (SCAI D–E) despite vasopressors/inotropes, with a plan (recovery, durable VAD, transplant or decision): fulminant myocarditis, massive PE with arrest/shock, post-cardiotomy shock, cardiotoxic poisoning (e.g. calcium-channel blocker, aluminium phosphide), refractory VT/VF storm, primary graft failure; and ECPR in selected refractory arrests.

steps.title: Screen contraindications
steps.detail: Absolute: no exit strategy (irreversible disease, not a transplant/VAD candidate). Relative: intracranial haemorrhage or major brain injury, contraindication to anticoagulation, >7 days of high-pressure ventilation (Pplat >30 and FiO₂ >0.9), advanced age or frailty, end-stage malignancy, severe immunosuppression. For VA: significant aortic regurgitation and aortic dissection.

steps.title: Call the ECMO centre early
steps.detail: Discuss with the regional ECMO team while the patient is still transportable; calculate RESP (VV) or SAVE (VA) to frame the discussion, not to decide alone.

tables.title: VV vs VA ECMO at a glance
rows: Femoral drainage (23–25 Fr) + internal jugular return (17–21 Fr), or a single dual-lumen bicaval cannula via right IJ
Peripheral: femoral venous drainage (21–25 Fr) + femoral arterial return (15–19 Fr) with a distal perfusion cannula (6–8 Fr); central (post-cardiotomy): RA + aorta
Enough for cardiac index ~2.2–2.5 L/min/m² (adult often 3–5 L/min); use the lowest flow that maintains perfusion
SaO₂ 85–92% often acceptable (mixing with native venous return)
Normal saturations; check the right radial ABG for differential hypoxia
Recirculation; hypoxaemia with high cardiac output
LV distension, differential (north–south) hypoxia, limb ischaemia
Pump the oxygenated blood through the lungs
Eject at least partly (aortic valve opening) to avoid LV stasis
tables.caption: Cannula sizes are typical adult ranges; the ECMO team chooses size from ultrasound vessel diameter and target flow.

tables.title: Common indications
rows: ARDS (viral, bacterial, aspiration), severe asthma, pulmonary haemorrhage/DAH, inhalational injury, chest trauma/contusion, large bronchopleural fistula, bridge to or after lung transplant

Selected AMI cardiogenic shock, fulminant myocarditis, massive PE, post-cardiotomy shock, decompensated cardiomyopathy as bridge, refractory arrhythmia, cardiotoxic poisoning, peripartum cardiomyopathy, hypothermic arrest, ECPR

redFlags.text: P/F <80 mmHg on FiO₂ 1.0 despite proning and paralysis: the ECMO window is closing — refer now.
Rising lactate, falling urine output and escalating vasopressor plus inotrope (SCAI C→D): mechanical support discussion must happen within hours.
New intracranial bleed or uncontrolled bleeding: anticoagulated ECMO may be lethal — consultant decision.
On peripheral VA ECMO: loss of arterial pulsatility with pink frothy secretions = LV distension; needs urgent unloading.

pitfalls.text: Starting ECMO before a genuine trial of prone positioning: ELSO lists a prone trial as part of optimal management unless contraindicated.
Choosing VV for a patient with severe septic cardiomyopathy: the native heart must still pump the oxygenated blood; echo first.
Referring after 7+ days of injurious ventilation: outcomes fall with longer pre-ECMO ventilation (a strong negative weight in RESP).

pearls.text: VV ECMO SaO₂ is rarely 100%: arterial saturation reflects the mix of oxygenated circuit blood and native venous return. 85–90% is often fine if oxygen delivery and lactate are adequate.
'Sweep for CO₂, flow for O₂': CO₂ clearance is controlled by sweep gas flow; oxygenation mainly by blood flow (and FdO₂).
Lower PaCO₂ slowly after initiation: rapid CO₂ falls are associated with neurological injury. ELSO suggests starting sweep around 2 L/min and titrating.

algorithm.title: Choosing ECMO mode
algorithm.description: Decision pathway from refractory organ failure to VV, VA or no ECMO.

nodes.text: Refractory respiratory and/or circulatory failure despite optimal conventional care
Realistic exit strategy (recovery, transplant, VAD, or bridge-to-decision)?
ECMO not appropriate: continue maximal conventional care; discuss goals with family
Active intracranial bleed, uncontrolled bleeding or contraindication to anticoagulation?
Consultant + ECMO centre risk–benefit discussion (heparin-free start possible in selected VV cases)
Echo: adequate cardiac function (no cardiogenic shock)?
Meets VV criteria? P/F <80 after prone trial, or pH <7.25 with RR 35 and Pplat ≤30
Optimise: prone ≥16 h, NMB, PEEP titration, conservative fluids; reassess within 6 h
Refer/initiate VV ECMO
Refractory cardiogenic shock (SCAI D–E) or refractory arrest meeting ECPR criteria?
Optimise inotropes/vasopressors, revascularise; consider Impella/IABP per indication
Refer/initiate VA ECMO with an LV-unloading plan

consultantNotes.pathophysiology:
**Oxygen delivery on ECMO.** Circuit O₂ supply = blood flow × (post- minus pre-oxygenator O₂ content). ELSO suggests a VV circuit able to supply at least 240 mL/m²/min of oxygen (rest requirement ~120 mL/m²/min; normal systemic DO₂ ~600 mL/m²/min). Because the circuit only oxygenates the fraction of venous return it drains, **SaO₂ on VV depends on the ratio of ECMO flow to native cardiac output** — a hyperdynamic septic patient can be hypoxaemic despite a perfectly working oxygenator.

**VA physiology.** Retrograde femoral arterial flow raises LV afterload. A weak LV may fail to open the aortic valve → LV distension, rising LA pressure, pulmonary oedema and stasis thrombus. If the heart recovers while the lungs are poor, deoxygenated blood ejected by the LV perfuses the coronaries and upper body (**differential or north–south hypoxia**).
consultantNotes.evidence:
**Respiratory ECMO**
- **CESAR (2009, UK):** referral to a single ECMO centre (75% actually received ECMO) reduced death or severe disability at 6 months (37% vs 53%). It tested *referral to an expert centre*, not ECMO itself.
- **EOLIA (2018):** early VV ECMO vs conventional lung-protective ventilation in very severe ARDS. 60-day mortality 35% vs 46% (RR 0.76; p=0.09), with 28% crossover to rescue ECMO in controls.
- **ELSO VV guideline (2021):** P/F <80 after optimal care including a prone trial, or pH <7.25 with RR 35 and Pplat ≤30; rest ventilator settings at minimum Pplat ≤25 cmH₂O and PEEP ≥10.

**Cardiac ECMO**
- **ECLS-SHOCK (2023):** routine VA ECMO in AMI cardiogenic shock with planned revascularisation did **not** reduce 30-day mortality (47.8% vs 49.0%) and increased moderate–severe bleeding and peripheral vascular complications.
- **ECMO-CS (2023):** immediate VA ECMO in rapidly deteriorating or severe CS did not improve the composite outcome vs early conservative therapy with rescue ECMO allowed.
- VA ECMO in AMI-CS is therefore for *selected* patients rather than routine use (ESC 2023 ACS guideline).
- **SCAI SHOCK stages (A–E)** give a shared language for escalation: C classic, D deteriorating, E extremis.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- **Age cut-off:** no threshold is defined; risk rises steadily with age.
- **Timing:** 'early' ECMO (EOLIA criteria) vs rescue — many Indian centres can only offer rescue because of cost.
- **Awake ECMO** and extubation on VV ECMO: attractive, but evidence is from cohorts.
- **VA ECMO in AMI-CS** after ECLS-SHOCK: limited to selected patients, arrest and mechanical complications.
- **Hybrid configurations** (V-AV, V-VA) for mixed failure need expert teams.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- ECMO is available mainly in tertiary private and some government institutes in large cities; most district and medical-college ICUs must **refer**. Build a referral relationship with your nearest ECMO centre before you need it.
- Cost is largely out-of-pocket; insurance and government-scheme coverage for ECMO varies — discuss realistic costs and duration (VV runs often last 1–3 weeks) with families early.
- Indian indications with a strong case for VA ECMO include **aluminium phosphide cardiotoxicity**, myocarditis, peripartum cardiomyopathy and massive PE; for VV, severe influenza/COVID-19 ARDS, leptospirosis pulmonary haemorrhage and scrub typhus ARDS.
- Leptospirosis pulmonary haemorrhage may need heparin-sparing strategies — a decision for the ECMO centre.

quiz.stem: A 34-year-old with influenza ARDS has P/F 68 mmHg on FiO₂ 1.0, PEEP 14, Pplat 29 after 18 h prone and cisatracurium. Echo shows normal LV and RV. The best mode of support is:
options: Inhaled nitric oxide only and wait 48 h
quiz.explanation: Isolated refractory hypoxaemic failure with adequate cardiac function = VV ECMO (ELSO: P/F <80 after optimal care including proning).

quiz.stem: On VV ECMO, which change most directly lowers PaCO₂?
quiz.explanation: CO₂ removal is controlled by sweep gas flow; oxygenation by blood flow and FdO₂.

quiz.stem: In ECLS-SHOCK (2023), routine VA ECMO in AMI cardiogenic shock:
options: Did not reduce 30-day mortality and increased bleeding
quiz.explanation: 30-day mortality 47.8% vs 49.0%, with more bleeding and vascular complications.

quiz.stem: On peripheral femoral VA ECMO, right radial SpO₂ is 82% while the post-oxygenator gas is normal and the femoral arterial PaO₂ is 300 mmHg. The likely cause is:
options: Differential (north–south) hypoxia from native lung failure
quiz.explanation: Native ejection of deoxygenated blood perfuses the upper body; improve native lung ventilation or convert to V-AV.

topics.title: ECMO referral: who, when and how
topics.summary: Practical referral criteria for respiratory and cardiac ECMO and ECPR, the scores used (Murray, RESP, SAVE), what the ECMO centre needs on the phone, and how to prepare for retrieval.

steps.title: Recognise the trigger
steps.detail: Respiratory: P/F <150 despite optimisation is the time to *call* (not necessarily cannulate); P/F <80, or pH <7.25 with hypercapnia, is the time to *act*. Cardiac: SCAI stage C not improving, or any stage D/E. ECPR: witnessed refractory arrest — call within the first 10–15 min of CPR.

steps.title: Phone the ECMO centre with an ISBAR summary
steps.detail: Age, weight, height, diagnosis and day of illness, days on ventilator, current settings (mode, FiO₂, PEEP, Pplat, RR, VT), ABG with P/F, prone/NMB done, vasopressor doses, echo, lactate, renal function, platelets/INR, neuro status, comorbidities, CT head if relevant, family wishes.

steps.title: Calculate Murray and RESP (VV) or SAVE (VA)
steps.detail: Murray lung injury score >3 was the CESAR referral trigger. RESP and SAVE estimate survival if ECMO is given; they support but do not replace clinical judgement.

steps.title: Prepare for cannulation or retrieval
steps.detail: Cross-match blood (at least 4 units PRBC or as the centre asks), check platelets, fibrinogen, INR; ask which vessels to keep free (often right IJ and both femoral veins); arterial line in the right radial for VA (upper-body oxygenation).

steps.title: If the patient is too unstable to move
steps.detail: Request mobile ECMO retrieval: the team cannulates at your bedside and transports on ECMO. Conventional transfer of a very hypoxaemic patient is high risk.

steps.title: Inform and consent
steps.detail: ECMO is a bridge, not a cure: explain likely duration, bleeding and stroke risk, cost, and the possibility of withdrawal if there is no recovery.

tables.title: Referral triggers (call the ECMO centre)
rows: P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6 despite optimisation, or proning needed
pH <7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥60 for >6 h despite RR 35
SCAI C with rising lactate or escalating drugs
SCAI D–E: refractory hypotension, worsening lactate, end-organ failure
Arrest or refractory shock despite (or contraindication to) thrombolysis
Witnessed arrest, shockable rhythm, good CPR
No ROSC after 10–15 min of ALS in an eligible patient
tables.caption: Thresholds summarise ELSO, EOLIA and CESAR entry criteria; local centres may differ.

tables.title: Typical ECPR inclusion criteria (centre-specific)
rows: Witnessed, with immediate bystander CPR (no-flow <5 min)
Initial shockable rhythm favoured; PE, hypothermia and poisoning also considered
ETCO₂ >10 mmHg, gasping or pupillary reaction during CPR favour candidacy
Unwitnessed arrest, end-stage disease, known DNAR, aortic dissection, severe AR, uncontrolled bleeding

tables.title: RESP score risk classes (survival on VV ECMO)
tables.caption: Pre-ECMO variables: age, immunocompromise, days of ventilation, diagnosis group, CNS dysfunction, non-pulmonary infection, NMB, nitric oxide, bicarbonate infusion, cardiac arrest, PaCO₂ and peak pressure.

redFlags.text: Do not wait for 'one more day' of conventional ventilation: pre-ECMO ventilation >7 days lowers survival and is a relative contraindication.
ECPR candidates need flow within ~60 min of collapse: call at minute 10–15, not minute 40.
Severe hypoxaemia during conventional transfer is dangerous — prefer mobile ECMO retrieval for the sickest patients.

pitfalls.text: Inserting a large central line in the right IJ when a bicaval dual-lumen cannula may be needed: ask the ECMO team which vessels to keep free.
Presenting a single ABG without ventilator settings: the centre needs P/F, PEEP, Pplat and proning status to judge reversibility.

pearls.text: CESAR showed the value of transfer to an experienced high-volume centre — the referral itself matters, even if the centre does not cannulate.
ECMO programmes work best in regional hub-and-spoke networks with mobile retrieval capability.

algorithm.title: ECMO referral pathway
algorithm.description: From deterioration to referral, retrieval or ECPR.

nodes.text: Severe respiratory or cardiac failure on maximal therapy
Refractory cardiac arrest now?
Meets local ECPR criteria (witnessed, bystander CPR, shockable/reversible cause, low-flow <60 min possible)?
Activate ECPR team now; continue high-quality (mechanical if available) CPR during transfer to cath lab/ECMO bay
Continue standard ALS; consider termination of resuscitation per guideline
Call ECMO centre: ISBAR summary, ABG + vent settings or haemodynamics + echo; calculate Murray/RESP/SAVE
Centre accepts?
Continue optimisation; agree re-discussion triggers and time
Safe for conventional transfer (oxygenating on transport ventilator, stable on modest vasopressor)?
Conventional critical-care transfer with senior escort
Mobile ECMO retrieval: cannulate on site, transfer on ECMO

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Reversibility is the key concept: ECMO buys time for the lung or heart to recover. Time on injurious ventilation causes fibroproliferation and reduces reversibility; each minute of low-flow CPR worsens hypoxic brain injury.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **ECPR trials:** ARREST (2020, n=30, refractory VF OHCA) stopped early: survival to discharge 43% vs 7% with ECMO-facilitated resuscitation in an expert system. Prague OHCA (2022) — invasive strategy including ECPR: 180-day good neurological survival 31.5% vs 22.0% (p=0.09). INCEPTION (2023, multicentre): 30-day good neurological survival 20% vs 16% (not significant).
- **AHA 2025 ALS:** ECPR may be reasonable for selected patients with refractory arrest when delivered within a skilled, organised system of care.
- **Scores:** RESP (VV) and SAVE (VA) were derived from ELSO registry data; discrimination is moderate and they were not designed to select or exclude individual patients.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- How far to transport a severely hypoxaemic patient conventionally vs waiting for retrieval.
- ECPR in Indian cities: long EMS response times and low bystander CPR rates mean most out-of-hospital arrests are not ECPR candidates; in-hospital witnessed arrests (cath lab, ICU, ED) are the realistic population.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Keep an updated list of regional ECMO centres and retrieval teams (phone numbers) on the ICU wall.
- Road transfer times in Indian cities are unpredictable; factor traffic into the choice between conventional transfer and mobile retrieval.
- Families often need time to arrange funds — start the conversation at the 'call' threshold, not the 'act' threshold.

quiz.stem: Which pre-ECMO factor most strongly lowers predicted survival in the RESP score?
options: Ventilation for more than 7 days before ECMO
quiz.explanation: Longer pre-ECMO ventilation (>7 days) carries a major negative weight; asthma, NMB use and viral pneumonia carry positive weights.

quiz.stem: A 45-year-old has a witnessed VF arrest in the cath lab with no ROSC after 12 minutes of ALS. In a centre with ECPR, the best next step is:
options: Activate ECPR while continuing high-quality CPR
quiz.explanation: Witnessed shockable refractory arrest within an ECPR system — activate early to keep low-flow time short.

quiz.stem: Before a planned bicaval dual-lumen VV cannula, which vessel should be kept free?
quiz.explanation: Dual-lumen bicaval cannulae are usually placed via the right IJ.

quiz.stem: CESAR primarily tested:
options: Referral to an ECMO centre vs conventional care
quiz.explanation: CESAR randomised to referral to a specialist centre for consideration of ECMO.

topics.title: IABP and Impella basics
topics.summary: How intra-aortic balloon pumps and microaxial flow pumps work, current evidence and indications, setting up and troubleshooting, and the checks each shift.

definition.text: IABP: a helium-filled balloon in the descending aorta that inflates in diastole (raising coronary perfusion pressure) and deflates just before systole (lowering afterload); adds roughly 0.5 L/min of cardiac output. Impella: a catheter-mounted microaxial pump that pulls blood from the LV and ejects it into the ascending aorta; CP delivers up to about 3.5–4 L/min, 5.0/5.5 up to about 5–5.5 L/min.

steps.title: Know when each device is used
steps.detail: IABP: mechanical complications of MI (acute MR, VSR) as a bridge, refractory ischaemia, selected high-risk PCI, LV unloading on VA ECMO. Routine IABP in AMI shock is NOT recommended after IABP-SHOCK II. Impella CP: selected STEMI cardiogenic shock (DanGer Shock), high-risk PCI, LV venting on VA ECMO ('ECPELLA'); Impella RP for RV failure.

steps.title: Confirm position
steps.detail: IABP tip 2–3 cm below the origin of the left subclavian artery — on CXR around the level of the carina / 2nd–3rd intercostal space. Impella: inlet in the LV below the aortic valve (about 3.5 cm for CP), outlet above the valve; confirm with echo and the console position waveform.

steps.title: IABP timing (check on 1:2)
steps.detail: Inflate at the dicrotic notch (aortic valve closure) → diastolic augmentation; deflate just before systole → assisted end-diastolic pressure lower than unassisted, and assisted systole lower than unassisted systole. Trigger: ECG (R wave) or arterial pressure.

steps.title: Anticoagulation
steps.detail: Impella: systemic heparin plus heparinised (or bicarbonate-based) purge per manufacturer/protocol. IABP: heparin commonly used, especially at 1:2–1:3 or prolonged support; unit protocols vary.

steps.title: Hourly device checks
steps.detail: Limb: distal pulses/Doppler, colour, temperature, sensation hourly. Left radial pulse and urine output (IABP migration can occlude the subclavian or renal arteries). Haemolysis (Impella): urine colour, plasma free Hb, LDH. Console alarms, purge pressure (Impella), helium supply (IABP).

steps.title: Wean and remove
steps.detail: IABP: reduce ratio 1:1 → 1:2 → 1:3 (or reduce augmentation) while haemodynamics and lactate stay stable; avoid prolonged 1:3 (thrombosis). Impella: reduce P-level stepwise with echo and haemodynamic checks. Remove with a haemostasis plan; check the limb afterwards.

tables.title: Temporary mechanical circulatory support compared
rows: Femoral (7–8 Fr); axillary for longer use
Afterload reduction, coronary perfusion; simple, cheap, widely available
Limb ischaemia, migration, balloon rupture, thrombocytopenia; no mortality benefit in AMI-CS
Direct LV unloading; DanGer Shock mortality benefit in selected STEMI-CS
Haemolysis, bleeding, limb ischaemia, AKI, malposition; high cost
LV distension, bleeding, limb ischaemia, stroke
tables.caption: Flows are approximate manufacturer ranges.

tables.title: IABP timing errors
rows: Inflation before the dicrotic notch; augmentation encroaches on systole
Premature aortic valve closure, ↑ LVEDV, ↑ afterload
Inflation well after the dicrotic notch; notch visible
Sharp drop after augmentation; assisted end-diastolic pressure may equal unassisted; U-shaped
Sub-optimal afterload reduction, possible retrograde coronary flow
Increased afterload and myocardial O₂ demand — most harmful

tables.title: IABP balloon size by patient height (typical manufacturer guide)
tables.caption: Manufacturer charts differ slightly; check the device insert. Many Indian adults need 34 mL rather than 40 mL.

redFlags.text: Loss of left radial pulse or left arm ischaemia with an IABP = balloon migrated too high; reposition urgently.
Sudden anuria with an IABP: consider low position occluding renal arteries (check CXR/ultrasound).
Blood (rust-coloured flecks) in the IABP helium tubing = balloon rupture: stop pumping, clamp, keep flat, arrange prompt removal (risk of entrapment).
Red urine or rising plasma free Hb on Impella: haemolysis — check position (echo), suction alarms, and reduce P-level.
Cold, pale, pulseless limb distal to a large-bore device: limb ischaemia — vascular surgery now.

pitfalls.text: Inserting an IABP 'routinely' for AMI cardiogenic shock: IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit; ESC advises against routine use.
Ignoring RV function before Impella CP: an LV pump cannot fill if the RV fails; check RV size/TAPSE and CVP.
Running an IABP at 1:3 for hours to 'wean': stasis promotes thrombus on the balloon; wean promptly or remove.

pearls.text: DanGer Shock (2024): Impella CP in STEMI cardiogenic shock (excluding comatose OHCA patients) reduced 180-day mortality 45.8% vs 58.5%, with more severe bleeding, limb ischaemia and RRT. Patient selection mattered.
On VA ECMO, an IABP or Impella can 'vent' the LV — consider when pulse pressure falls below ~10 mmHg or the aortic valve stops opening.

algorithm.title: Escalating mechanical support in cardiogenic shock
algorithm.description: Simplified decision tree for temporary MCS (heart-team decisions).

nodes.text: Cardiogenic shock (SCAI C+) despite optimal drugs; revascularise if ACS
Mechanical complication of MI (acute MR, VSR, free-wall rupture)?
IABP (or Impella/ECMO) as bridge to urgent surgery
Predominant RV failure?
Optimise RV (preload, pulmonary vasodilators, inotropes); consider Impella RP or VA ECMO
Severe hypoxaemia, cardiac arrest or biventricular failure?
VA ECMO with LV-unloading plan (IABP/Impella)
STEMI-CS, not comatose after OHCA, LV-dominant?
Consider Impella CP (DanGer Shock population) in an experienced centre
Heart-team decision: Impella vs VA ECMO vs continued medical therapy; avoid routine IABP

consultantNotes.pathophysiology:
**IABP:** diastolic inflation displaces ~30–50 mL of blood, raising aortic diastolic pressure (coronary perfusion); deflation lowers aortic end-diastolic pressure and LV afterload. Its effect needs a native rhythm and some LV function, and is blunted in tachyarrhythmias.

**Impella:** draws blood from the LV into the aorta continuously, lowering LV end-diastolic pressure and volume (myocardial O₂ demand) while increasing forward flow — 'unloading'. Suction events occur with hypovolaemia, RV failure or malposition against the LV wall.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **IABP-SHOCK II (2012):** 600 patients with AMI-CS undergoing early revascularisation; IABP did not reduce 30-day mortality (39.7% vs 41.3%), and later follow-up showed no long-term benefit.
- **DanGer Shock (2024):** 360 STEMI-CS patients; Impella CP reduced all-cause death at 180 days (45.8% vs 58.5%; HR 0.74). The composite of serious adverse events (severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, device failure, worsening aortic regurgitation) was more frequent, as was RRT.
- **ESC 2023 ACS:** routine IABP not recommended in CS without mechanical complications; short-term MCS may be considered in selected patients.
- **SCAI stages** guide timing: escalation is usually considered at stage C not responding, or D.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Impella outside the DanGer Shock population (e.g. NSTEMI-CS, comatose OHCA) remains uncertain.
- Routine LV venting on VA ECMO: observational data suggest benefit; randomised evidence is limited.
- IABP retains a role in resource-limited settings for mechanical complications and as a bridge, given low cost and familiarity.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- IABP is widely available in Indian cath labs and is often the only device in tier-2 cities; use it for evidence-based indications (mechanical complications, bridge) rather than routinely.
- Impella is limited and expensive in India; mainly found in large cardiac centres.
- Many Indian adults are of shorter stature: check balloon size against height (34 mL is common).

quiz.stem: On a 1:2 IABP trace, the assisted end-diastolic pressure is higher than the unassisted end-diastolic pressure. This indicates:
quiz.explanation: Late deflation means the balloon is still inflated as the LV starts ejecting, increasing afterload — the most harmful error.

quiz.stem: After IABP insertion the left radial pulse disappears. The most likely cause is:
options: Balloon migrated too high, occluding the left subclavian
quiz.explanation: The tip should lie 2–3 cm below the left subclavian origin; upward migration can occlude it.

quiz.stem: DanGer Shock showed that Impella CP in STEMI cardiogenic shock:
quiz.explanation: 180-day death 45.8% vs 58.5%, with more bleeding, limb ischaemia and RRT.

quiz.stem: Which is a contraindication to IABP?
quiz.explanation: Diastolic inflation worsens regurgitant flow in significant AR; aortic dissection is another contraindication.

topics.title: Daily ECMO checks and rounds
topics.summary: A structured patient-and-circuit checklist for every ECMO patient: neurology, haemodynamics, pump, oxygenator, anticoagulation, ventilator 'rest', and the daily plan.

steps.title: Patient: neurology and sedation
steps.detail: Pupils, GCS/RASS off sedation where possible, focal signs; low threshold for CT head (ICH risk). Aim for light sedation once stable; awake ECMO when possible.

steps.title: Haemodynamics and perfusion
steps.detail: MAP (VA: usually 65–80 mmHg), pulse pressure (VA: >10 mmHg suggests LV ejection), lactate, urine output, cannulated-limb perfusion with Doppler and NIRS if available. Pre-oxygenator saturation is a venous surrogate on VV but is distorted by recirculation.

steps.title: Circuit: pump and flow
steps.detail: Record RPM, blood flow and their relationship (rising RPM for the same flow = drainage problem or circuit resistance). Look/listen for line 'chatter' (shaking drainage line = hypovolaemia or cannula obstruction). Drainage (pre-pump) pressure is normally kept less negative than about −100 mmHg.

steps.title: Circuit: oxygenator
steps.detail: Pre- and post-oxygenator pressures and the gradient across the membrane (rising ΔP = clot); post-oxygenator blood gas daily (PO₂ should be very high on FdO₂ 1.0); inspect connectors and oxygenator with a torch for clot and fibrin; check gas line, blender, heater temperature.

steps.title: Anticoagulation and blood
steps.detail: Anti-Xa or aPTT, ACT if used, platelets, fibrinogen, INR, Hb, LDH, plasma free Hb, bilirubin; antithrombin if heparin resistance. Common targets: Hb ≥7–8 g/dL (higher if DO₂ inadequate), platelets >50 × 10⁹/L (higher if bleeding), fibrinogen >1.5 g/L.

steps.title: Ventilator 'rest' settings (VV)
steps.detail: Pplat <25 cmH₂O (≤30 acceptable), PEEP ≥10, low RR (4–30), FiO₂ 0.3–0.5; avoid hyperoxia and VILI. Track compliance and tidal volume at a fixed driving pressure, plus CXR.

steps.title: Echo and imaging
steps.detail: VA: LV size, aortic valve opening, LV/aortic-root smoke or thrombus, RV, pericardial collection. VV: cannula position (dual-lumen jet towards the tricuspid valve), RV function. CXR: cannula position, lung opacity.

steps.title: Whole-patient care
steps.detail: Infection screen (heater masks fever), early enteral nutrition, skin and pressure areas, physiotherapy/mobilisation, CRRT integration if used, drug dosing (circuit sequesters lipophilic drugs such as fentanyl, midazolam, propofol), family update.

steps.title: Daily goals and weaning screen
steps.detail: Can sweep or FdO₂ be weaned (VV)? Is there native cardiac recovery (VA)? Write today's targets: SpO₂, PaCO₂, MAP, anti-Xa, fluid balance.

doseCards.dose: Bolus 50–100 units/kg at cannulation; infusion about 7.5–20 units/kg/h titrated to target
doseCards.target: anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 units/mL (or aPTT ~1.5–2.5 × baseline) per unit protocol; lower targets if bleeding
doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg at 10 units/kg/h = 700 units/h = 1.4 mL/h of 500 units/mL
doseCards.verify: Targets vary between ECMO centres; follow the unit protocol.

tables.title: ECMO round checklist (bedside chart)
rows: MAP, pulse pressure (VA), lactate, urine output
Right radial ABG (VA), patient ABG, post-oxygenator ABG
SaO₂ ≥85–88% on VV; post-oxy PO₂ high; PaCO₂ corrected slowly
Stable RPM:flow; drainage pressure less negative than about −100 mmHg
ΔP pre/post, clots, sweep, FdO₂, gas line
Rising ΔP or visible clot = plan change
Plasma free Hb, LDH, urine colour
Sites, sutures, dressing, depth marks, limb perfusion
Weaning trial? Family update? Exit strategy?

redFlags.text: Rising membrane pressure gradient, falling post-oxygenator PO₂ and rising D-dimer/plasma free Hb = oxygenator failing: plan a change before it fails.
Shaking drainage line with falling flow: hypovolaemia, tamponade, pneumothorax, cannula malposition or abdominal compartment — do NOT just increase RPM.
Unequal pupils or sudden GCS drop: urgent CT head (intracranial haemorrhage); hold anticoagulation per consultant.
Cold, mottled cannulated leg on VA: check distal perfusion cannula flow; vascular surgery review.

pitfalls.text: Relying on aPTT alone: on ECMO it is confounded by coagulopathy, low fibrinogen and inflammation; anti-Xa is more specific for heparin effect.
Missing infection because there is no fever: the heat exchanger holds blood temperature; watch WBC, inflammatory-marker trends and new organ dysfunction.
Unexplained under-dosing of sedatives and antibiotics: circuit components sequester lipophilic and highly protein-bound drugs; use TDM where available.

pearls.text: Recirculation on VV: pre-oxygenator saturation rises towards post-oxygenator saturation while patient SaO₂ falls. Increase cannula tip distance or adjust flow; check with echo.
Keep an 'emergency card' at each ECMO bed: emergency ventilator settings, clamp locations, hand-crank instructions and the ECMO specialist's phone number.

algorithm.title: Low flow or 'chattering' circuit
algorithm.description: Troubleshooting falling ECMO flow with drainage-line vibration.

nodes.text: ECMO flow falling and/or drainage line shaking
Reduce RPM until chatter stops; keep minimum safe flow; call ECMO specialist
Kink, clot or cannula displacement visible?
Relieve kink / secure cannula; check depth marks and imaging
Echo: tamponade, pneumothorax, collapsed IVC/RA or cannula malposition?
Treat cause: drain tamponade, chest drain, reposition cannula under echo
Hypovolaemia likely (bleeding, diuresis, vasodilation, CRRT removal)?
Give 250–500 mL crystalloid, or blood if Hb low; treat bleeding; review CRRT net removal
Consider abdominal compartment syndrome (bladder pressure), high intrathoracic pressure, coughing/agitation (sedate)
Restore flow gradually; document the new RPM:flow baseline

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: **Pressures in a centrifugal circuit.** Pre-pump (drainage) pressure is negative; the more negative, the greater the suction on the vein (haemolysis, chatter, cavitation). Pre-oxygenator pressure is the highest in the circuit; post-oxygenator pressure reflects return-cannula resistance and patient afterload. The gradient across the oxygenator rises as the membrane clots.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **ELSO VV 2021** gives ventilator 'rest' ranges (Pplat <25 recommended, ≤30 acceptable; PEEP ≥10; RR 4–30; FiO₂ 0.3–0.5) and notes variable transfusion practice (some target Hb >7 g/dL, others up to 12 g/dL; restrictive practice may be considered).
- **ELSO Anticoagulation 2021:** heparin first-line; DTIs (bivalirudin, argatroban) for HIT or heparin resistance; no single monitoring test is perfect, so centres should use a consistent protocol combining tests.
- Daily structured checklists are expert-consensus practice to reduce missed complications.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Haemoglobin target on VV ECMO (7 g/dL vs higher) — oxygen delivery depends on both Hb and flow.
- Anti-Xa vs aPTT vs viscoelastic tests (TEG/ROTEM) for monitoring.
- Low-dose or anticoagulation-free VV ECMO in bleeding patients is increasingly used with modern coated circuits.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Anti-Xa assays may not be available 24/7 in many Indian labs; agree an aPTT/ACT-based fallback protocol.
- Plasma free Hb is not routinely available in many hospitals — use LDH, bilirubin and urine-colour trends as surrogates.
- Oxygenators and circuits are expensive; early recognition of rising ΔP allows a planned (safer) change.

quiz.stem: On VV ECMO the pre-oxygenator saturation has risen from 65% to 88% and patient SaO₂ has fallen from 90% to 80% at unchanged flow. The most likely problem is:
quiz.explanation: Returned oxygenated blood is being drained straight back into the circuit.

quiz.stem: The pressure gradient across the oxygenator has doubled over 24 h. This suggests:
quiz.explanation: Rising pre-to-post oxygenator ΔP indicates increasing resistance from thrombus.

quiz.stem: The recommended VV ECMO 'rest' plateau pressure in ELSO 2021 is:
quiz.explanation: ELSO recommends Pplat <25 cmH₂O (≤30 acceptable) with PEEP ≥10.

quiz.stem: Why can fever be absent in an infected ECMO patient?
options: The heat exchanger controls blood temperature
quiz.explanation: The heater/cooler holds blood at its set temperature, masking fever.

topics.title: ECMO complications and emergencies
topics.summary: Recognition and first actions for air in the circuit, pump failure, decannulation, bleeding, LV distension, differential hypoxia, haemolysis, thrombosis, limb ischaemia and HIT.

steps.title: Call for help and protect the patient
steps.detail: Call the ECMO specialist/perfusionist and consultant. VV: switch the ventilator to the pre-agreed emergency settings (e.g. FiO₂ 1.0, PEEP 10–15, VT ~6 mL/kg PBW, RR 20–30). VA: prepare for CPR and vasopressors if flow stops.

steps.title: Air in the circuit
steps.detail: Clamp the return line close to the patient (then the drainage line) and stop/minimise the pump; if air may have entered the arterial circulation (VA), head-down left-side position and 100% O₂. De-airing and restart are specialist tasks. Find the source (loose connector, open port, cavitation from very negative drainage pressure).

steps.title: Pump or power failure
steps.detail: Check power and plug into mains/UPS; if the pump head or console fails, clamp, move the pump head to the hand crank and turn at the previous RPM until a back-up console is connected.

steps.title: Accidental decannulation
steps.detail: Clamp the circuit, apply firm pressure to the site, emergency ventilator settings (VV) or CPR/vasopressors (VA), activate massive transfusion, call surgeon/ECMO team for recannulation.

steps.title: Bleeding
steps.detail: Find the site (cannula, surgical, airway, GI, intracranial). Check platelets, fibrinogen, anti-Xa/aPTT and TEG/ROTEM if available. Reduce or hold heparin (consultant), give platelets (often to >80–100 × 10⁹/L if bleeding) and fibrinogen (>1.5–2 g/L), consider tranexamic acid. Intracranial haemorrhage: stop anticoagulation, neurosurgical opinion.

steps.title: LV distension on VA
steps.detail: Signs: pulse pressure <10 mmHg, aortic valve not opening, LV dilatation/smoke on echo, pulmonary oedema. Act: lowest adequate ECMO flow, add dobutamine, avoid high afterload (MAP ~65), consider IABP or Impella venting, or atrial septostomy.

steps.title: Differential (north–south) hypoxia on femoral VA
steps.detail: Right radial SpO₂/ABG low while the lower body is well oxygenated. Act: improve native lung (FiO₂, PEEP, secretion clearance), or convert to V-AV (add a return limb to the IJ) or central cannulation.

steps.title: Haemolysis and thrombosis
steps.detail: Haemolysis: rising plasma free Hb/LDH, dark urine — check drainage pressure (too negative), clot in pump head (noise, heat), oxygenator thrombus; change component. Thrombosis: visible clot, rising ΔP, DVT at cannula sites, LV/aortic-root thrombus (VA), limb ischaemia.

doseCards.dose: 1 g over 10 min, may follow with 1 g over 8 h
doseCards.notes: Reduce dose in renal failure; watch the circuit for clot.
doseCards.verify: Use on ECMO is based on observational data; consultant decision.

doseCards.dose: Start about 0.025–0.05 mg/kg/h; titrate to aPTT 1.5–2.5 × baseline
doseCards.verify: Reduce in AKI; follow ECMO centre protocol.

doseCards.role: Inotrope to promote LV ejection on VA ECMO

tables.title: ECMO complications: recognise and respond
rows: Pressure, local haemostatics, suture review, correct coagulopathy, reduce heparin
CT; stop anticoagulation; neurosurgery; BP control
Dark deposits, rising ΔP, falling post-oxy PO₂, rising D-dimer
Plan oxygenator/circuit change; review anticoagulation, antithrombin, HIT
pfHb >50 mg/dL, LDH ↑, red/brown urine, AKI
Check drainage pressure, pump head, oxygenator; adjust flow/cannula; change component
Pulse pressure <10, aortic valve closed, pulmonary oedema
Distal perfusion cannula; vascular surgery; fasciotomy if compartment syndrome
New organ dysfunction, rising inflammatory markers (fever masked)
Cultures from the patient, source control, PK-guided antibiotics
Stop all heparin (including flushes), start DTI, send PF4 antibodies
Mucosal bleeding despite acceptable routine tests
Consider vWF assays; resolves after decannulation
CRRT via the circuit or separately; avoid overload

redFlags.text: Air in the return line: CLAMP NOW — arterial air on VA can cause massive stroke and coronary embolism.
Sudden loss of flow with no power: hand crank immediately — know where it is stored.
New neurological deficit or pupil change: CT head; intracranial haemorrhage is among the most lethal ECMO complications.
Pink frothy ETT secretions on VA ECMO: LV distension with pulmonary oedema — urgent unloading.
Platelets falling >50% from day 5–10 of heparin: think HIT; switch to a direct thrombin inhibitor while testing.

pitfalls.text: Turning up RPM to fix low flow: worsens negative pressure, haemolysis and cavitation without treating the cause.
Taking ABGs from the left radial or a femoral line on femoral VA: these mostly reflect circuit blood; the right radial best represents coronary/cerebral oxygenation.
Continuing heparin flushes after HIT is suspected: stop every heparin source.

pearls.text: Everyone on the unit should know three things: where the clamps are, where the hand crank is, and each ECMO patient's emergency ventilator settings.
A distal perfusion cannula placed at femoral VA cannulation reduces limb ischaemia; check its flow every shift.

algorithm.title: Sudden hypoxaemia on VV ECMO
algorithm.description: Stepwise troubleshooting when patient SaO₂ falls on VV ECMO.

nodes.text: Patient SaO₂ falls on VV ECMO
Flow and sweep as set? Gas line connected and FdO₂ 1.0?
Reconnect gas, check blender/cylinder, restore flow
Post-oxygenator PO₂ low?
Oxygenator failure: urgent change; emergency vent settings meanwhile
Pre-oxygenator saturation high (recirculation)?
Reposition cannulae under echo/X-ray; adjust flow
High cardiac output / high VO₂ (fever, sepsis, agitation, shivering)?
Cool, deepen sedation ± paralysis, treat sepsis; consider more flow or higher Hb
Native lung worse: check ETT, pneumothorax, secretions, effusion; raise vent FiO₂/PEEP temporarily
Reassess SaO₂ and lactate; document plan

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Blood contact with the circuit triggers contact activation, inflammation and consumption of platelets and fibrinogen; high shear degrades large vWF multimers (acquired von Willebrand syndrome). At the same time, stasis zones and foreign surfaces promote thrombosis — ECMO patients bleed and clot simultaneously.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- Bleeding and thrombosis are the commonest ECMO complications in registry reports; intracranial haemorrhage carries very high mortality.
- **ECLS-SHOCK** and **DanGer Shock** both showed more bleeding and vascular complications with device therapy, underlining careful selection and vascular technique (ultrasound-guided access, distal perfusion cannula).
- **ELSO Anticoagulation 2021** supports direct thrombin inhibitors when heparin is contraindicated (HIT) or ineffective.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Routine vs on-demand LV venting on VA ECMO.
- Prophylactic vs reactive distal perfusion cannulation.
- Anticoagulation-free periods for bleeding on VV ECMO — increasingly accepted with modern coated circuits.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Run regular ECMO emergency drills (air, pump failure, decannulation); staff turnover is high in many Indian ICUs.
- Test UPS/back-up power and generator change-over; power fluctuations are common in some regions.
- Keep a spare oxygenator, pump head and hand crank in the unit.

quiz.stem: You see a column of air in the return line of a VA ECMO circuit. The first action is:
options: Clamp the return line close to the patient and call for help
quiz.explanation: Clamp to stop arterial air embolism, then de-air under specialist control.

quiz.stem: On femoral VA ECMO, pulse pressure is 4 mmHg, the aortic valve stays closed and pink froth appears in the ETT. Which response is NOT appropriate?
options: Reduce ECMO flow to the lowest adequate level
Increase noradrenaline to raise MAP to 95 mmHg
quiz.explanation: Raising afterload worsens LV distension; aim for MAP around 65 and unload the LV.

quiz.stem: Platelets fall from 220 to 80 × 10⁹/L on day 7 of heparin on ECMO with a new cannula-site DVT. The next step is:
options: Stop all heparin, start bivalirudin or argatroban, send PF4 antibodies
quiz.explanation: Intermediate–high 4Ts probability of HIT: switch to a DTI pending tests.

quiz.stem: The pump console loses power and does not restart. What do you do immediately?
options: Start CPR on a VV patient
Clamp and hand-crank the pump head at the previous RPM
quiz.explanation: Hand-cranking maintains flow until a back-up console is connected.

topics.title: Weaning and decannulation
topics.summary: Judging readiness and running trials off VV and VA ECMO, echo criteria for VA weaning, decannulation, and care afterwards.

steps.title: Screen readiness (VV)
steps.detail: Improving CXR and compliance; FiO₂ ≤0.6, PEEP ≤10, PaO₂ ≥70 mmHg on the ventilator; ventilation achievable with VT ≤6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤28, RR ≤28 (ELSO criteria).

steps.title: VV wean: FdO₂, then sweep
steps.detail: Reduce FdO₂ stepwise from 1.0 to 0.21 (about 20% steps) keeping SpO₂ >92% or PaO₂ ≥70; then reduce sweep by 0.5–1 L/min steps to 1 L/min; then sweep OFF (gas capped) for a trial of several hours, checking ABG, work of breathing and haemodynamics.

steps.title: Screen readiness (VA)
steps.detail: Cause reversed/recovering, MAP ≥65 with pulsatility on reduced flow, low inotrope/vasopressor needs, normal lactate, adequate oxygenation on the ventilator (FiO₂ ≤0.5).

steps.title: VA wean: flow reduction with echo
steps.detail: Reduce flow stepwise (e.g. 0.5–1 L/min steps) to ~1–1.5 L/min with adequate anticoagulation. At minimum flow, echo predictors of success in one cohort: LVEF >20–25%, aortic VTI ≥10 cm, lateral mitral annulus peak systolic velocity (TDSa) ≥6 cm/s; plus stable MAP and no RV dilatation.

steps.title: Decannulate
steps.detail: Plan with the team: stop heparin per protocol beforehand; VV cannulae are usually removed percutaneously with a purse-string/figure-of-8 suture and pressure; the VA arterial cannula usually needs surgical repair or a closure device. Have blood available.

steps.title: Post-decannulation care
steps.detail: Duplex for cannula-associated DVT (common), limb checks after arterial decannulation, restart thromboprophylaxis when safe, watch for re-deterioration, start rehabilitation and family follow-up.

doseCards.verify: Evidence for ECMO weaning is observational/small RCTs; consultant decision.

doseCards.role: Inodilator for RV/LV support during weaning

tables.title: Conditions for a VV weaning trial (ELSO 2021)
rows: PaO₂ ≥70 on ≤6 L/min nasal cannula/face mask, or HFNC ≤40 L/min with FiO₂ ≤0.3
VT ≤6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤28, RR ≤28; acceptable pH/PaCO₂ without excessive work of breathing
Acceptable pH without excessive work of breathing

tables.title: Echo predictors of successful VA weaning at minimal flow
tables.caption: From Aissaoui et al. 2011 (single-centre cohort); combine with clinical judgement.

redFlags.text: SpO₂ falls or respiratory rate rises above ~35 with sweep off: trial failed — resume support; do not 'push through'.
RV dilatation or MAP fall during VA flow reduction: not ready; restore flow and reassess in 24 h.
At very low VA flow (<1–1.5 L/min), circuit thrombosis risk rises: keep trials short and anticoagulated.

pitfalls.text: Testing VV readiness by cutting blood flow to very low levels: reducing gas (FdO₂, sweep) with preserved blood flow avoids low-flow circuit thrombosis.
Forgetting cannula-associated DVT after decannulation: screen with duplex and anticoagulate if present.

pearls.text: A sweep-off trial tests both oxygenation and CO₂ clearance by the native lungs; many centres observe for several hours before decannulation.

algorithm.title: VV ECMO weaning trial
algorithm.description: ELSO-based gas-weaning pathway with preserved blood flow.

nodes.text: Daily screen on VV ECMO
Meets ELSO trial conditions (FiO₂ ≤0.6, PEEP ≤10, PaO₂ ≥70, VT ≤6 mL/kg, Pplat ≤28, RR ≤28, improving CXR)?
Continue support; rescreen tomorrow
Wean FdO₂ 1.0 → 0.21 in ~20% steps (SpO₂ >92% / PaO₂ ≥70)
Wean sweep in 0.5–1 L/min steps to 1 L/min; ABG each step
Sweep off (gas capped) for several hours: ABG, RR, work of breathing, haemodynamics
Stable gas exchange and work of breathing?
Resume previous sweep/FdO₂; identify the reason (fluid, secretions, weakness)
Plan decannulation with the team; stop heparin per protocol

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: VV weaning tests whether the native lungs can oxygenate and clear CO₂ at safe ventilator settings. VA weaning tests whether the native heart can generate adequate output against normal afterload — reducing flow increases preload and lowers afterload, unmasking true LV/RV function.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **ELSO VV 2021** provides explicit weaning-trial conditions and a gas-flow weaning sequence with preserved blood flow.
- **VA weaning:** Aissaoui et al. (2011) found that at minimal flow, aortic VTI ≥10 cm, LVEF >20–25% and TDSa ≥6 cm/s predicted successful weaning.
- Levosimendan has been associated with better VA weaning success in observational cohorts; randomised data are limited.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Duration of sweep-off trials (2 h vs 24 h).
- Decannulation while intubated vs after extubation on ECMO.
- Pump-controlled retrograde trial off (PCRTO) for VA weaning — limited evidence.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Financial pressure to decannulate early is real for many families; still follow objective criteria — failed early decannulation followed by recannulation is costlier and more dangerous.
- Arrange vascular surgical support for VA arterial decannulation in advance.

quiz.stem: In the ELSO gas-weaning approach for VV ECMO, which parameter is reduced first?
options: FdO₂ (oxygen fraction delivered to the oxygenator)
quiz.explanation: Stepwise FdO₂ reduction from 1.0 to 0.21, then sweep reduction, with blood flow preserved.

quiz.stem: Which echo finding at minimal VA flow predicts successful weaning?
options: Aortic VTI ≥10 cm and TDSa ≥6 cm/s
quiz.explanation: Aissaoui criteria: VTI ≥10 cm, LVEF >20–25%, TDSa ≥6 cm/s.

quiz.stem: A common complication to screen for after VV decannulation is:
quiz.explanation: Cannula-associated DVT is common; duplex screening is advised.

drugs.name: Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
drugs.indications: Standard circuit anticoagulation on VV/VA ECMO; IABP and Impella systemic anticoagulation
drugs.adultDose: Cannulation bolus 50–100 units/kg IV (many centres use about 5,000 units). Infusion typically started at 7.5–20 units/kg/h once bleeding is controlled, titrated to anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 units/mL or aPTT about 1.5–2.5 × baseline (unit protocol). Low-intensity targets (anti-Xa 0.2–0.3 units/mL) or temporary holds are used on VV ECMO with active bleeding.
drugs.preparationIndia: 5,000 units/mL vials (1 mL and 5 mL). Common infusion: 25,000 units in 50 mL NS = 500 units/mL.
drugs.renalHepatic: No renal adjustment. Antithrombin deficiency causes heparin resistance (high dose needed, low anti-Xa).
drugs.cautions: HIT (check platelets daily; 4Ts if fall >50%). Bleeding. aPTT is unreliable on ECMO (confounded by coagulopathy, low fibrinogen, inflammation); prefer anti-Xa where available.
drugs.monitoring: anti-Xa or aPTT 6-hourly until stable then 12–24-hourly; ACT at bedside only as a crude check; platelets, fibrinogen, antithrombin if resistance.
drugs.verify: Target ranges and starting infusion rates differ between ECMO centres; align to the unit's written protocol.

drugs.name: Bivalirudin
drugs.indications: Anticoagulation on ECMO when HIT is suspected/confirmed or heparin resistance
drugs.adultDose: No bolus usually; start about 0.025–0.05 mg/kg/h and titrate to aPTT 1.5–2.5 × baseline (reported ranges up to ~0.2 mg/kg/h; reduce in renal failure and per protocol on CRRT).
drugs.preparationIndia: 250 mg lyophilised vial; e.g. 250 mg in 50 mL NS = 5 mg/mL.
drugs.renalHepatic: Partly renally cleared: reduce dose substantially in AKI.
drugs.cautions: No reversal agent. Stasis areas of the circuit (and stagnant blood in the LV on VA) can clot because the drug is cleaved locally.
drugs.monitoring: aPTT (or dilute thrombin time where available) 4–6-hourly initially.
drugs.verify: Dosing ranges come from observational ECMO data and vary widely; use only with an ECMO-centre protocol.

drugs.name: Argatroban
drugs.indications: Alternative anticoagulant for HIT on ECMO
drugs.adultDose: Critically ill/ECMO: start low, about 0.2–0.5 mcg/kg/min (standard HIT dose 2 mcg/kg/min is often too high in critical illness and hepatic dysfunction); titrate to aPTT 1.5–3 × baseline.
drugs.preparationIndia: Limited availability and costly in India; check pharmacy.
drugs.renalHepatic: Hepatic clearance: markedly reduce in liver dysfunction or congestion.
drugs.verify: Low-dose ECMO starting rates are from case series; confirm with haematology.

drugs.name: Dobutamine
drugs.indications: VA ECMO: maintain LV ejection/aortic valve opening and prevent LV distension; low-output states during weaning trials
drugs.preparationIndia: 250 mg/20 mL ampoule; 250 mg in 50 mL = 5,000 mcg/mL.
drugs.cautions: Tachyarrhythmias, myocardial oxygen demand, hypotension from beta-2 vasodilation.
drugs.monitoring: Heart rate and rhythm, arterial pulse pressure, echo LV ejection.

drugs.name: Milrinone
drugs.indications: RV support, LV support on VA ECMO, weaning
drugs.adultDose: 0.125–0.5 mcg/kg/min IV infusion; loading dose usually omitted in shock (hypotension).
drugs.preparationIndia: 10 mg/10 mL ampoule; 10 mg in 50 mL = 200 mcg/mL.
drugs.renalHepatic: Renally cleared: reduce to 0.125–0.25 mcg/kg/min in AKI.
drugs.cautions: Hypotension, arrhythmias, long half-life (longer in AKI).

drugs.name: Levosimendan
drugs.indications: Facilitating VA ECMO weaning (observational data); low-output states
drugs.adultDose: 0.05–0.2 mcg/kg/min IV for 24 h, usually without bolus in hypotensive patients.
drugs.preparationIndia: 12.5 mg/5 mL vial; 12.5 mg in 500 mL D5W = 25 mcg/mL.
drugs.renalHepatic: Active metabolite persists about a week; avoid in severe renal/hepatic impairment.
drugs.verify: Use for ECMO weaning rests on observational and small randomised data; consultant decision.

drugs.name: Tranexamic acid
drugs.indications: Significant bleeding on ECMO/MCS (cannula site, mucosal, post-cardiotomy)
drugs.adultDose: 1 g IV over 10 min, may follow with 1 g over 8 h; reduce in renal impairment.
drugs.renalHepatic: Reduce dose in renal impairment (seizure risk).
drugs.cautions: Theoretical circuit/oxygenator thrombosis; seizures at high doses.
drugs.monitoring: Circuit inspection for clot, oxygenator pressure gradient.
drugs.verify: ECMO-specific evidence is observational; consultant decision.

drugs.name: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine)
drugs.indications: MAP support on ECMO (usual MAP target 65–80 mmHg on VA ECMO; avoid excess afterload)
drugs.adultDose: 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min IV via central line; titrate to MAP.
drugs.preparationIndia: 2 mg/2 mL ampoules (check whether the label states base or bitartrate). Common: 4 mg in 50 mL = 80 mcg/mL; 8 mg in 50 mL = 160 mcg/mL.
drugs.cautions: On peripheral VA ECMO excess vasopressor raises LV afterload and can stop aortic valve opening.
drugs.monitoring: Arterial line, pulse pressure, echo, limb perfusion.
